passage:
You asked me on the show, Zainab, whether my parents ever found out I was reading about other religions at fifteen. I'm Lalit. Yes, my mum did. She found the library books under my mattress and went white. "Who is putting this in your head?" I stopped telling her anything for a month.
But my uncle, who was there that night, sat with me later and simply asked, "What's pulling you towards it?" I said I wanted to know why people believe different things. He didn't panic. He gave me the names of a few books and said I could ask him anything, any time. I still tell him almost everything, even what I don't tell my friends.

qa.q: What did Lalit's mum find under the mattress?
qa.a: She found the library books under the mattress.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling after the mother's reaction, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Lalit felt shut out and wary, since Lalit stopped telling the mum anything for a month.

qa.q: What did Lalit's uncle do that kept the door open?
qa.a: The uncle asked calmly what was pulling Lalit toward it, gave a few book names and said Lalit could ask anything any time.

qa.q: How might Lalit's mum have been feeling when she found the books and went white?
qa.a: She was probably frightened and worried, not angry for its own sake, and reached for a question that came out as blame.

grounding: A teenager explores religion out of real curiosity; panic makes it go underground and calm answers keep the door open.

passage:
I'm Damini, and I live next door to Jahnavi's family. One evening I heard her mother's voice through the wall and braced for shouting. Jahnavi had been watching videos of teenagers jumping off high walls, and she wanted to try one.
Her mother said, "Show me one. I'd like to see what you like about it." They watched together. Then she asked, "What worries you about it? What would make it safer?" Jahnavi said the jumps looked fun, but the girl in the last video limped away. They talked about the climbing wall a local club runs, with helmets and ropes.
I can't know what Jahnavi felt, but she laughed later on the stairs, and she still asks her mother about things.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi watching videos of?
qa.a: Jahnavi was watching videos of teenagers jumping off high walls.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have felt when her mother asked to watch the video?
qa.a: Jahnavi was probably surprised and relieved not to be told off, and so more willing to talk about the risk.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi's mother do that kept the conversation open and also protected Jahnavi?
qa.a: She asked to see what Jahnavi liked, watched together, asked what worried Jahnavi and pointed to a safer option, the climbing wall with helmets and ropes.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi's mother have been feeling as she asked to watch the video?
qa.a: She was probably worried but steady, choosing curiosity over shouting, since she asked what worried Jahnavi and pointed to a safer option.

grounding: A teenager is curious about risky videos; a parent's calm response keeps the door open and steers toward safety.

passage:
Friday
Went with Rehana to her family's Eid prayers at the mosque near her house. I just watched from the side. It was so calm. Everyone moving together. I asked Rehana a hundred questions after.
At dinner I asked Papa why we don't pray like that, and whether God is the same for everyone. His face changed. "Who is putting these ideas in your head? You're not going there again." Mummy went quiet.
So I stopped talking and went to my room.
Later, Dadi came in with a glass of milk. She sat on my bed and said, "Tell me what you saw." I told her everything. She listened, then told me about the Sufi songs she loved as a girl. She said questions about God are old and good, and that I can ask her anything.
I'm going to ask Dadi, not Papa. For now.
Kunal

qa.q: Where did Kunal go with Rehana?
qa.a: To her family's Eid prayers at the mosque near her house.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel after Papa's reaction?
qa.a: Kunal felt shut down and hurt, and went quiet to hide the curiosity.

qa.q: What did Dadi do that kept the door open?
qa.a: She came in calmly, asked what Kunal saw, listened, shared her own memories and said questions about God are old and good.

qa.q: How might Papa have seen Kunal's question?
qa.a: Papa probably felt worried or threatened, fearing Kunal was being influenced, and reacted with panic instead of curiosity.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring religion from real interest, whose curiosity goes quiet when met with panic but stays open with a calm listener.

passage:
Ankita: can I ask u something weird
Abhinav: always
Ankita: people at school keep joking about "consent". I actually don't get what it means properly. and I can't ask mummy, she'll freak
Abhinav: not weird at all. good question
Abhinav: it means both people clearly and freely agree to something, like a hug or holding hands or anything more. and either person can change their mind anytime
Ankita: even if they said yes before?
Abhinav: yes. a yes can become a no, and that has to be respected
Ankita: ok that makes sense. why don't they teach this properly
Abhinav: they should. the school counsellor is good for this stuff btw, and maybe try asking your mum calmly, she might surprise you
Ankita: maybe. thanks for not being weird 🙂
Abhinav: ask me anything, anytime

qa.q: What were people at school joking about?
qa.a: Consent.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel about asking her mother?
qa.a: Ankita felt nervous, sure that Mummy would freak out if asked.

qa.q: What did Abhinav get right in that answer?
qa.a: Abhinav stayed calm, gave a clear age-fit answer, and pointed to the school counsellor and Mummy as trusted adults.

qa.q: What would change if Abhinav had panicked at the question?
qa.a: Ankita might have stopped asking and looked for answers in less reliable places.

grounding: Shows a teenager curious about a sensitive topic, and a calm answer that keeps the conversation open.

passage: In the small town of Bijnor, Samir, fifteen, spent every evening watching videos of stunt riders doing wheelies on highways. His aunt Parveen khala found him on the roof, phone glowing. Samir tensed, waiting for shouting. Instead she sat down. "What do you like about them?" He shrugged. "They're free. Brave." "They look brave," she said. "Do you want to try?" He hesitated. "Maybe." Parveen didn't panic. She told him about her college friend who broke both legs on a road like that. Then she said, "If you're serious about bikes, there's a proper training ground in Meerut with gear and coaches. We'll talk to your abbu tonight." At dinner she did. Abbu listened, and agreed Samir would not ride on the highway, and they would visit the training ground together on Sunday. Samir kept watching videos, but now he showed them to her.

qa.q: Where is the proper training ground Parveen khala mentioned?
qa.a: In Meerut.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when Parveen khala found him on the roof?
qa.a: He was tense, expecting to be shouted at for watching the videos.

qa.q: What did Parveen khala do that kept Samir talking to her?
qa.a: She stayed calm, asked what he liked, shared a real story of the risks, and brought in his abbu that evening with a safe plan.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt when Parveen raised it at dinner?
qa.a: He was probably worried but glad to know, and relieved there was a safe plan to agree on.

grounding: Shows a teenager curious about risky stunt videos, and an adult's calm response keeping the door open instead of driving it underground.

passage: Olga found the books under Oskar's bed in their Gdańsk flat while looking for a lost sock: a Quran in Polish, a book on Buddhism, and a street preacher's pamphlet about the end of the world. Her first feeling was panic. Nobody in their family went to any church. She put the books back and waited until dinner. "I saw your books," she said. "I'm not angry. What got you interested?" Oskar went red, then shrugged. "Everyone at school is so sure about everything. I want to know why." "The end-of-the-world one worries me a bit," Olga admitted. "It worries me too," he said. "That's why I kept it." They talked until the soup went cold. Afterwards he left the Buddhism book on the kitchen table, not under the bed.

qa.q: Where did Olga find the books?
qa.a: She found them under Oskar's bed in their Gdańsk flat.

qa.q: How did Oskar feel when Olga mentioned the books?
qa.a: He was embarrassed at first and went red, but seemed relieved when she wasn't angry and he could explain his curiosity.

qa.q: What made Olga's approach keep the door open?
qa.a: She waited until she was calm, said she wasn't angry, asked what got him interested and admitted her own worry honestly.

qa.q: What would change if Olga had thrown the books away in a panic?
qa.a: Oskar would likely hide his questions and read in secret, with no one to talk to about the pamphlet that worried him.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring religions and a worrying pamphlet out of real interest, and a parent's calm questions keeping talk open.
